Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our technique has also been successfully applied to two distinct TCN architectures and demonstrates its versatility.

Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like soundness and completeness in reasoning about incomplete datasets. Building on this foundation, we address the issue of soundness and develop a method for determining the truth of individual facts, which we prove to be both sound and complete. Additionally, we investigate the challenge of querying such datasets and explore the difficulty of ensuring sound results. To make an exception, we present a efficient solution for sound three-way classification and the verification of facts, as well as a sound Composed Program (CP) query, which however turns out to be undecidable. To illustrate our approach, we provide an efficient non-monotonic logic program that can reason about four categories of facts, and we investigate the difficulty of sound query answering in this context. To address this difficulty, we develop a novel, decidable, complete subclass of CP, which we use to enhance the original program and obtain soundness of query answers. To illustrate our approach, we address the issue of soundness and completeness of reasoning about incomplete datasets.

This task becomes particularly challenging due to the combinatorial nature of variable clustering, which is compounded by the need to account for variable combinations rather than individual variables. To address this difficulty, we propose a new framework and corresponding measurement tool called "cluster signal-to-noise ratio" (CSNR) that takes into consideration both the p-value achieved in a given test and the combinatorial complexity of variable subsets. The CSNR concept leads to an innovative and intuitive explanation of existing importance measures, such as BIC and information distance, in variable selection problems. Leveraging the CSNR concept, we can derive combinatorial importance guarantees for existing methods, such as LASSO and FDR control, and establish new "local" importance conditions that are less stringent than traditional relevance conditions. The CSNR framework also paves the way for the development of new combinatorial importance measures and associated algorithms.

By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration. However, obtaining precise measurements demands both a densely packed stellar catalog and the elimination of systematic errors. This study utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate the sources of systematic errors in relative photometry, including variations in exposure time, flux normalization, and point spread function estimation. With a simulated catalog of 10^5 stars observed across 100 fields, it was found that the mean and variance of the ratio between observed flux and model stellar flux introduce the largest source of systematic error, contributing approximately 0.01 to the RMS of the derived aerosol depth. Since this approach does not necessitate prior assumptions about the stellar population, it has significant implications for calibrating observations and can be applied to any method of relative photometry.

multi-phonon physics, has been largely dependent on theoretical understanding due to its elusive nature and difficulty in conducting precise experimental measurements. yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, conferring an advantage over other single-photon catalyzed states in terms of both quantum capability and production efficiency, as catalytic parametric amplifiers require less power than catalytic beam splitters.

CT scans with low resolution is complicated, particularly when the esophagus is narrowed or when there are foreign objects present. This challenge is exacerbated in 3D scans, as the search for tumors is limited to a narrow tube-like structure. To mitigate this issue, researchers have traditionally focused on converting 3D scans into 2D images for analysis. However, this process often discards valuable information contained within 3D images. This study proposes a novel approach that directly processes 3D images using the L-Flow network, which incorporates boundary and lumen features from various angles to enhance tumor identification accuracy. The results show that this direct processing method significantly outperforms traditional methods that indirectly process 3D images.

Employing 4D seismic monitoring to track fluid movement and pinpoint wellbore deviations necessitates precise seismic imaging and wellbore path knowledge.  Although seismic data can image subsurface anomalies, its poor wellbore resolution poses challenges in correlating seismic interpretations with wellbore observations, and detecting wellbore deviations and stimulations near the wellbore is difficult.  To mitigate  migration smearing and improve seismic data accuracy and reliability, reverse time imaging is used to image wellbore anomalies, and imaging the wellbore directly with high-frequency, dense logging while imaging is conducted is also beneficial.  A successful integration of seismic imaging and down- wellbore logging is demonstrated at the Iona field, where an anomalous bioturbated zone associated with water coning was imaged and confirmed through direct wellbore observation, and the complex fracture network created by natural and induced stimulation of an enhanced horizontal well could not be seen through standard imaging techniques but was clearly visible using 4D seismic and validated through direct wellbore observation.  These results demonstrate that direct4D seismic stimulation and validation can offer valuable insights into subsurface character and evolution, and the implications of this for optimizing reservoir management and recovery strategies are discussed.

task in natural language processing, which involves identifying and classifying pre-defined entities within text. A significant aspect of this process is recognizing the boundaries of entities. Traditional methods for NER can be divided into two categories: rule-based approaches and statistical methods. Rule-based approaches rely on manually established rules and handcrafted features, whereas statistical methods utilize probabilistic models or representations learned from data to predict entity boundaries. Given the extensive range of techniques for training statistical models, they will not be explored in detail here. Instead, this survey focuses on model architectures for entity boundary prediction. Specifically, it examines models based on text, language, knowledge, and adversarial frameworks, as well as evaluation metrics and datasets used to assess model performance in predicting entity start and end positions.

groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, potentially non-bipartite rearrangements of the same bipartite graph can yield significantly lower edge crossings. Our research aims to address this challenge by presenting an innovative rearrangement algorithm specifically tailored for bipartite graphs that require fewer crossings than their non-bipartite counterparts. The proposed method guarantees an $O(n^{2.5})$ edge-crossings layout, whereas the well-established Four-Rooks Theorem enables achieving $O(n^2)$ edges-crossings in bipartite graphs, but with vertex repetitions that are undesirable in graph drawings. The algorithm we developed arranges each graph's vertex without repetition while ensuring a desirable $O(n^{2.5})$ edge-crossings condition.

It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Moreover, determining the minimum number of unknotting operations required to transform a given knot into an unknot is a non-trivial task, which is referred to as the unknotting number, and this problem has been shown to be NP-hard. In recent years, numerous methods have been developed to address this challenging problem, including both exact and approximate solutions. In this study, we tackle the unknotting operation problem from a graph theory perspective, by formulating it in terms of graph minors, and by exploring the relationship between the unknotting operation and the rank of a chordal graph associated with a knot diagram.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper re-examines the origins of proposal selection issues in FPNs, proposing that the problem stems from a lack of mid-sized feature extraction capability within the framework. This is attributed to a mismatch between the available proposal scales and the geometric progression of FPN scales, which inherently favors either small-scale detection at the cost of mid-size accuracy or the promotion of mid-size detection, which in turn makes it difficult to identify larger objects. This analysis is further validated through mid-sized object detection being correlated with proposal selection issues and demonstrated through experimentation. The proposed Solution is to introduce an additional mid-sized scale to fill this gap, which is straightforward to implement and effective at detecting mid-sized objects, which in turn makes it easier to detect larger objects as a result. This is further corroborated through mid-size detection being correlated with optimal proposal variance, which can also be observed in natural images, where it aligns with object size distributions and can be used to guide optimal scale design.

We apply this approach to learn temporal connections from highly ordered natural videos and validate it against a widely-used dataset featuring pre-defined temporal sequences. Following this, we evaluate our approach on a more challenging dataset with ambiguous event sequences and uncontrolled settings. To test its ability to generalize to unfamiliar scenes, we conduct additional experiments comparing our results to human judgments about event sequencing. Our findings show that our method achieves a strong correlation with human reasoning about event sequences in both controlled and natural environments.

we've found that using small groups of lithium ions trapped vertically in an electrostatic trap can effectively minimize energy dissipation, or 'heating,' of the electrons. This small configuration, or resonance mode, keeps energy contained within the ion layer and allows it to persist for a long time using a simple two-dimensional model of electrons and ions. In contrast, a more complex, three-dimensional simulation shows that disrupting this small configuration by shaking the electrons' velocity along the trap's electric field leads to the formation of an electron heat trail, or phase-space hole, outside the ion layer. This phenomenon has not been observed before in laboratory settings. However, introducing a static shift in velocity along the trap's field can stabilize the small configuration by altering its charge balance. This stability can be explained through an effective force that takes into account the influence of electrons' non-Maxwellian behavior. Surprisingly, this stability shift in velocity can be recovered when including magnetic effects, as long as the magnetic field is sufficiently strong.

The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a couple of application examples. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that extract features frame by frame but fail to capture long-range dependencies within action semantics. Moreover, they often suffer from low resolution matching due to the typical downsampling of features to fixed dimensions. To address these issues, we introduce two innovative components into the boundary matching framework. Firstly, the Multi-Granularity Feature Fusion module fuses features across multiple granularities using a tree structure, facilitating feature fusion from non-adjacent frames and providing multi-scale features to boost boundary localization. increased interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. This novel technology employs the use of passive surface elements to optimize signal paths on a dynamic wireless network. In this paper, we investigate an optimization problem for the downlink of an IRS-assisted communication system. Specifically, our objective is to maximize the minimum signal-to-interference-plus noise ratio among all legitimate users by adjusting the passive surface coefficients. However, this optimization problem poses significant challenges due to its non-convex nature and non-concave objective function. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a new multi-start semidefinite relaxation method, along with an efficient check to minimize the relaxation gap. To complement this, we also propose a low-complexity perturbation check to reduce the relaxation domain. Furthermore, in order to address potential local optima caused by the NP-hard nature of the problem, we introduce an iterative proximal penalty method that can converge to a high-quality solution with a reduced number of iterations.

To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel method that efficiently leverages both task-specific and pre-trained features through what is known as quadratic attention. This study reveals that these failures can be foretold by a sudden, minor drop in velocity less than a microsecond before the final breakdown. This minor velocity drop becomes more pronounced as the applied stress increases, and its magnitude varies between different samples, indicating diversity in material flaws. This minor velocity drop is associated with non-catastrophic cracking within the material. Comparing the minor and catastrophic cracking velocities, researchers found the minor crack propagation is significantly slower, around 1 to 100 meters per second, while the catastrophic crack propagation approaches the lasing sound speed, typically 1 to 5 times the sound speed. These observations suggest that the minor and catastrophic events are driven by pre-existing microcracks, which aligns with prior theories, and also indicates that a dynamic Weibull distribution may be a suitable model for predicting the reliability of binary oxide lasers.

Sketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances its robustness properties. Notably, the larger quadratic factor can be circumvented by reducing the sketch size, thus making the number of iterations linear in the dimensionality of the vector being identified. Our findings can be applied to a wide range of scenarios involving the identification of large components in vectors, including finding the heaviest path in graphs and estimating frequent items in distributions. Our research also identifies ideal dimensions for sketching scenarios depending on the number of queries made.

we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. As a primary task, accurate depth estimation from monocular images depends on capturing distant objects. Constrained by camera specifications, vehicles are rarely positioned directly above such objects. This challenge challenges current neural networks that struggle to generalize when conditions vary. To address this issue, we introduce a novel learning framework called Far-Field Objects Detection and Estimation (FOODE) that first trains the object's 3D properties using orthographic projection before fine-tuning for the visible perspective projection. The FOODE method allows for both supervised and weakly supervised approaches, and our experiments on diverse object categories show the effectiveness of our method. The results indicate that the proposed framework can train objects at great distances without needing 3D labels and produce more precise depth predictions compared to current field-of-view-based methods. Notably, the proposed method can detect four-legged objects from above and from the side, a capability that is critical for autonomous vehicles.

A specific class of nuclear molecules, known as transition metal to CO (TMCO) molecules, exhibit a peculiar phenomenon called the "linear CO inversion" (LCI), in which the CO molecule flips from its standard orientation to a backwards one. While imaging algorithms can generate migration residuals, they are computationally expensive and not seamlessly integrated with physics-based forward modeling tools. This study introduces a novel, bidirectional connection between migration residual computation and adjoint-source modeling via a numerically stable reordering of operations, achieved via a combination of algebraic manipulations and application of Gaussian elimination. This research focuses on higher-order harmonics in the Blandford-Payne model of a magnetic disk, specifically electromagnetic waves emitted by an infinitely thin, steady-state disk. This link was previously identified in a previous study by the authors and their colleagues, but was restricted to a specific case. In this study, we extend the analysis to a broader range of parameters within the four-band Hubbard model, and examine the fractional Chern insulator state for various types of repulsive interactions and different magnetic flux patterns in the unit cell. By employing a variational approach, we map out the phase diagram of a two-component Chern insulator under different conditions and discover that the optimal Chern state is sensitive to the specific repulsive interaction considered. This optimal state can be described using both local and non-local ansatz, and exhibits a superconducting tendency that emerges from the local pair-correlation function. This finding confirms and expands the initial conclusion that the superconducting tendency is linked to the Chern state, as it is found to occur over a broader parameter range. Topic modeling has emerged as a powerful tool for identifying the underlying structure within large bodies of text. It extracts latent themes from collected information and assigns labels to facilitate further processing. However, traditional topic models have struggled to cope with ever-increasing data volumes. To tackle this challenge, we have devised a method for incrementally updating a topic model, which can process information in real-time and efficiently navigate large datasets. By presenting the data in a streaming format, our approach allows for the sequential computation of a probabilistic model, which in turn enables the use of effective point-of-interest techniques, such as search and navigation. By comparing our results to batch-trained models, we have shown that our method yields comparable accuracy while offering significant performance benefits. Additionally, our approach has been shown to be versatile across a range of datasets. However, its true potential is unlocked when applied to real-world information that spans the web.

Community compositions varied across time periods and were influenced by sex, with male users more likely to be among the most active participants. However, the impact of sex on community structure differed across sub-communities, with female users more likely to form their own clusters on the "For Women Only" community. Furthermore, we discovered that the most active users were those with higher education levels and higher income. To mitigate the limitations of self-selected samples and observe behavior outside of controlled settings, conducting studies on online interactions is crucial. Consequently, this research holds significant value for examining how the youth engage with politics on Instagram and can inform policy decisions on digital citizenship.

However, a significant challenge lies in reconciling often conflicting stellar parameters derived from various methods. This difficulty stems from the diverse approaches used to extract such parameters, which focus on different stellar properties and make assumptions that vary widely. A common strategy involves analyzing individual spectra, yet this method suffers from limitations such as spectrum distortion and computational intensity. An alternative, comparison with synthetic models through various matching criteria, although producing more consistent and model-dependent results, is also prevalent. To address these issues, we developed a versatile and robust statistical framework capable of integrating multiple stellar indicators, yielding precise, coherent, and stellar-mass-dependent parameters for a broad range of stellar populations. This innovative approach was applied to the M67 open star cluster, using a high-quality, high-resolution, high-signature array from the KEPLER field, to test its effectiveness. The results demonstrated an exceptionally small dispersion of stellar parameters specific to M67, and when applied to the solar neighborhood and the LMC, the method maintained its effectiveness. Notably, the method is entirely automatic, does not yield model-dependent outcomes for individual stars, and can be adapted to analyze any stellar population without requiring significant adjustments.

By comparing these radii to those of younger galaxies and those around them, the study aims to determine how the physical sizes of galaxies have changed over time. This problem is compounded by the varying levels of human skill and the difficulty in directly comparing human demonstrations. These challenges underscore the importance of leveraging multiple, uncurated, human demonstrations for RL agents. In this paper, we address the task of aggregating human demonstrations from diverse sources, each characterized by varying levels of skill. Our research builds on previous work on demonstration aggregation from expert models, where teachers are assumed to be error-free. In contrast, in this study, human teachers are not assumed to be optimal, variation-prone, and comparison-free. Specifically, we formulate the problem of demonstration aggregation as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where multiple, variation-prone, and comparison-free teachers provide demonstrations. Our proposed algorithm, Demonstration Aggregation via Q-Learning (DAQL), learns transition and reward functions from these teachers, whose preferences are unknown, uncomparable, and potentially contradictory. DAQL then learns an optimal policy that maximizes the reward without needing to understand or reconcile human preferences. Our experimental evaluations on grid worlds and robotic tasks show that DAQL significantly outperforms baseline approaches in demonstrating better alignment with multiple, diverse human preferences.

By allowing energy from the resonance to build up in the post-bounce shock layer, we see how it can interact with the standing-accretion-shock mechanism. As the scalar field concentration grows, it causes neutrino-flux bursts that are amplified by the resonance. These bursts are then affected by the scalar field's modification of the radiation's mean free path. In both cases, the presence of a companion for a theory results in an enhanced understanding of the meta-theoretical properties of that theory. Specifically, if a theory has a companion, it is consistent with infinitely many cardinals exceeding its own cardinality, whereas a theory without a companion is either finite or exhibits a distinctive finiteness or boundedness across all infinite cardinals exceeding its own cardinality. Online forums, often referred to as OAFs, provide platforms where people openly discuss their experiences, sharing personal stories and seeking advice. By analyzing such social networks, we aim to predict the abuse of opioids, which has crucial public health implications. Furthermore, we discovered that the model learns to focus on the most relevant information and connections, providing insight into the complex relationship between online behavior and the abuse of opioids.

For the case of the Sun and Earth, this effect is minuscule compared to other phenomena, making it a useful analogy for compact binary systems consisting of an intermediate mass object and a compact companion.  In this study, we investigate the impact of tidal forces on the accretion and evolution of such systems, assuming the inner object is surrounded by a circumbinary disk.  We simulate disk evolution using a one-dimensional model that incorporates mass loss due to the object's companion, and we observe the system's behavior as it evolves from the solar system's mass range to that of a black hole.  When the disk remains in hydrostatic equilibrium, mass loss causes a slow, continuous growth of the central object, and this process can occur at any stage of evolution, from early on to when it is surrounded by a supermassive black hole.  However, if mass loss accelerates beyond the companion's three-body resonance threshold, we see either disk ejection or the formation of an inner disk around the central compact object.  This phenomenon has significant implications for the growth of black holes and neutron stars, as well as for the formation of supermassive black holes.  These processes may also be responsible for creating a broad mass spectrum of black holes and neutron stars, and for the observed reverber mapping of broad-line.

In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Our research reveals the impact of different norms on the network's behaviour and leads to the conclusion that networks trained with the less restrictive the $L_1$-norm possess greater accuracy than those trained with the more stringent $L_\infty$-norm. The results of the simulation were compared with the existing observational data from three different observational windows, and the results revealed that the planet's nightside temperature is at least 450 K and possibly even as high as its dayside temperature, and that further observational data on this planet's spectral characteristics may indicate the presence of ice clouds in the atmosphere.

studying the unique magnetic properties of insulating materials with unpaired electrons, especially those with magnetism arising from localized electron interactions. A significant challenge in understanding these materials lies in resolving conflicting models that describe charge, spin, and orbital degrees of freedom. One area of investigation is SmNiO3, a material with a nearby metal-insulator transition, offering a unique opportunity to study the interplay between these materials' constitutive factors. In this study, we developed a comprehensive model of effective electrons based on the materials' underlying electronic structure, taking into consideration electron-electron interactions, structural distortions, and dielectric fields. The results reveal that for a sudden electron release, spin disorder appears as a hallmark of the materials' insulating state, while the application of an external dielectric field gradually lowers the spin disorder, accompanied by the development of orbital order and increased electron localization. Notably, this orbital order persists until the materials transition from an insulating to a metallic state. Our comprehensive approach highlights the potential of using effective electron models as intuitive tools for exploring complex multidimensional phase diagrams within these complex materials.

Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of handling multiple types of constraints in presence of conflicting signals. This study presents an original framework called Multi-Constrained Imitation Learning (MCoIL) to accommodate various signal sources, including environmental and kinematic constraints, and demonstrates its ability to manage complex scenarios where signals conflict with one another. The MCoIL framework formulates learning from demonstrations and constraints as a joint optimization problem, along with an artificial barrier function to prevent unnecessary signal interference. An innovative data augmentation technique has been proposed to facilitate convergence to an optimal solution and avoid local minima. The algorithm has been theoretically analyzed for global and local convergence, and practical applications have been tested on two cases: an underactuated mobile robot with conflict between constraints and an industrial manipulator with conflict between constraints and demonstrations. The results indicate that MCoIL outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multi-constrained imitation learning problems.

To effectively solve these systems in a computationally efficient manner, domain decomposition algorithms are utilized, allowing for the scaling of computations across multiple finite element grids. In addition to solving these nested structures, this research also accounts for large discontinuities in material properties. In order to solve these problems, new BDDC and AMG BDDC solvers are developed and successfully applied to a set of test problems. However, the reliability of such indicators has been shown to vary depending on the nature of the transition. This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of characteristic frequency as an early warning signal for gradual onsets in one-dimensional nonspatial populations. By analyzing both theoretical and simulated data, the findings indicate that the characteristic frequency's ability to accurately predict gradual onsets is limited, with its reliability significantly compromised near the critical threshold. galaxies at various stages of evolution in a cosmological simulation, revealing the interplay of star formation, gas dynamics, and black hole activity. In the early stages of galaxy development, intense star formation triggered by gravitational collapse occurred within dense gas clusters, although this was temporarily suppressed by the activation of central supermassive black holes. In the middle stages of galaxy evolution, a powerful outflow from the active black hole temporarily disrupted a vast amount of gas, fostering the birth of numerous young star clusters. In the final stages of galaxy evolution, a powerful jet from the supermassive black hole pushed a vast amount of gas and created a long-lived shockwave that persisted for millions of years, effectively regulating the birth of new stars and influencing the relationship between the mass of the black hole and the mass of galaxy bulges. Our visual and observational evidence demonstrates the universal impact of feedback mechanisms from supermassive black holes on the life cycle of galaxies within a high-resolution, radiation-hybrid hydrodynamics simulation.

As a result of this, there's an increased interest in studying such decays thoroughly. In the Standard Model, radiative decays of $P$ mesons involve electromagnetic penguin diagrams, which could provide an indicator of new physics. In this study, we examine LFU in the radiative decays of $B_c$ mesons within the framework of the quark model and investigate the impact of hadronic effects through phase space integrations using the complex quark-antiquark potential model. Our analysis considers four scenarios: independent motion, correlated motion, independent motion with spin effects, and correlated motion with spin effects for both $P$ and $\Sigma$ mesons. We calculate $b$-quark initiated and sea-quark initiated processes and compare their contributions. We find that sea-quark initiated contributions are significant and cannot be disregarded. Moreover, we observe that new physics effects manifest differently in various decay channels due to their reliance on different quark emission probabilities. Consequently, combining analyses of $e^0$ and $\mu^0$ modes allows us to mitigate uncertainties associated with hadronic effects and new physics signals become more apparent across all hadronic effects considerations.

By applying a dynamic topological model, we identify the key structural characteristics of various representative systems and demonstrate that these characteristics align with those of a fully connected network. Conversely, in the presence of external disturbances, systems with high topological homogeneity allow graph neural networks to capture both the dominant coherent dynamics and a regular pattern of network oscillations, which act as noise reducers. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats severe epilepsy by removing intractable brain lesions.  Monitoring the surgery's impact on adjacent healthy brain tissue requires functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).  To make real-time 3D brain imaging in real-time during LITT possible, a high-performance imaging sequence has been developed and optimized for the therapy's changing frequency environment. This new sequence, combined with an advanced imaging protocol and robust reconstruction algorithm, enables real-time, 3D epilepsy brain imaging at approximately 2 Hz. The process is also adaptable for other surgeries embedded in the brain, allowing for precise, real-time removal of abnormal brain regions, while minimizing damage to healthy adjacent tissue.

modeling often involves dealing with a substantial and high-dimensional set of variables. Despite its widespread use in various fields, a common class of models, known as the generalized additive models, has not fully developed specialized estimation methods to handle this problem. To address this limitation, a specialized additive screening procedure has been developed, building on an existing variable screening method. This new procedure enables efficient dimension reduction and variable selection for generalized additive models with categorical data. Simulation experiments and real-world data analysis show that this new method produces reliable estimates, generates accurate predictions, and outperforms some conventional benchmark models.

This issue stems from inefficient texture sampling due to arbitrary coordinate usage, exacerbating issues with real-time rendering and visual perception. To tackle this, our research focuses on developing a custom filtering method that prevents artifacts while maintaining or enhancing sharpness, considering how humans perceive shapes and edges. on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 14 ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs). These galaxies are undergoing intense star formation and are shrouded in dense dust. Our spectral data covered a wide range from optical to infrared wavelengths. Our primary goal was to study how mass within ULIRGs moves due to their dynamic processes. Our analysis techniques included comparing the velocity fields of galaxies using vector difference maps, estimating non-gravitational forces using the Fisher equation, and conducting thorough case-by-case examinations. Our findings indicate that galaxies in the sample possess sufficient mass within their central regions to account for increased mass within their outer areas, unless there are large gas outflows. Our data also provided constraints on the presence of outflows in three galaxies. Additionally, we identified signs of gas movement in almost all of the observed ULIRGs, which may complicate our mass calculations. Our further observations suggest that galaxies in the sample may not be perfectly stationary, and may be affected by other factors such as gas inflows, merging, or asymmetries in mass distribution. Ultimately, our study emphasizes the significance of considering the interaction between mass and dust within ULIRGs when interpreting their behavior.

~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, which contains at most~$k$ elements, and constitutes a strong geodetic subset of~$G$. This problem is known to be NP-complete for specific graph types, including chordal graphs. Notably, the runtime of the algorithm is determined by~$p$, which represents the length of the longest shortest path in~$G$. Although this problem has been found to be NP-complete even within distance-two perfect graphs, a strong connection with the strong metric dimension was also discovered. Any algorithm capable of solving the strong geodetic problem can be applied to solve the strong metric dimension problem. A new algorithm with an exponential time complexity was devised for solving the strong geodetic problem in perfect graphs, and this approach runs at a speed determined by~$p$. Additionally, a previous algorithm was improved, leading to a more efficient solution with a running time of $O(1.8167^n)$ for the strong metric dimension problem on general graphs.

While there has been significant progress in imitation learning through distance-minimization approaches using supervised learning, these methods struggle to incorporate the crucial aspect of accumulating long-term rewards. In contrast, reinforcement learning methods like reward maximization are capable of leveraging past experiences for future success but rely on a precise and predefined reward function that is often unavailable in imitation learning scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a method that effectively combines the strengths of both methods by directly learning from an implicit reward function represented by a value function. By leveraging the expert cost function and learned dynamics, we show that our approach can accurately recover the underlying reward function and, consequently, the optimal policy for the task at hand. To prove the efficacy of our method, we apply it to multiple sequential decision-making tasks in both static environments and robotic manipulation scenarios using the IsaacGym simulator, and our experimental results reveal superior performance compared to baseline methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical application of our approach on a real-world task using a grabbing task with a gripper controlled by multiple continuous variables.

In contrast, leveraging peer information by incorporating other agents' experiences seems like a promising approach, particularly in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Unfortunately, direct usage of peer data is problematic as the contexts and actions it contains are unlikely to be relevant to the target task. Existing methods that extract high-quality behavior from peers involve extensive demonstrations or further imitation learning, incurring substantial costs. In contrast, our proposed method efficiently leverages peer information by transforming previously collected peer experiences into the target context through a context transformation network. However, this network risks overfitting and promoting irrelevant peer behaviors. To mitigate these issues, our method introduces a discriminator that identifies and suppresses incoherent peer experiences. Moreover, we introduce a mutual information term that enables the context transformation network to focus on relevant peer information. Our method's components are optimizable via a standard loss function, resulting in an efficient use of peer experiences. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments on the PZT benchmark and Minecraft game, where it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/THU-MLGroup/EFIL.

In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a comprehensive framework to quantify and explore the impact of biases present in 2D chest X-ray datasets using a medical image classification task.  Our study reveals that datasets contain significant labels-independent information, often unrelated to medical conditions, and unbalanced distributions of image characteristics across normal and abnormal classes. These models utilize the maximum likelihood framework to estimate parameters and assess uncertainty via standard errors and Wald tests. However, these methods typically ignore the impact of correlation among the observations of individual animals. A common scenario in habitat selection studies involves the same animals being observed in various habitats over time. This leads to repeated measurements and potential dependency within the data set. Ignoring this dependency can result in a form of 'pseudo-replication', which may inflate the apparent sample size, leading to a underestimation of standard errors and an overestimation of statistical significance. A new model is proposed to account for observation correlation, with random animal effects used to model individual-specific variation. This model alternative allows for a more accurate estimation of standard errors and model comparison via AICc. A simulation study was conducted to show that the proposed random animal effects model yields a more accurate estimation of standard errors, p-values, and hypothesis testing outcomes than the standard model that ignores observation correlation. An application of the proposed model is demonstrated using habitat selection data of female gray wolves in Yellowstone National Park.

To establish this, we develop a perturbation theory framework that accounts for both classical and quantum correlations between matrices. This framework enables precise comparison of expected trace values $\mathbb{E}[\tr(A_1 A_2 \cdots A_k)]$ with those of free random matrices whose entries have centered distributions. Specifically, let $A_1, \dots, A_k$ be independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices, and for each $j$, define the random variable $a_j = A_j/N$ such that $\mathbb{E}[\tr_j(A_j)] = 0$. Then, the difference between the actual and free expectations scales as $O(N^{-2})$. Furthermore, if $a_1, \dots, a_k$ were asymptotically free, then for any fixed $r$, the difference scales as $O(N^{-2} + N^{-r})$. This result is applied to analyze expected norms of Gelfand-Toisson kernels on random Hermitian and unitary matrices, providing novel insights into these complex systems.

This process is often simplified for second-order operators as it is possible to check for constant coefficient equivalents. However, for operators of higher order, such a straightforward approach is not feasible, and determining the compatibility conditions becomes a distinct mathematical challenge. We discuss various strategies to approach this problem, including examining the symbol of the operator, and present multiple new methods, such as utilizing Riemann's approach or considering operators defined on limited domains. Ultimately, finding the compatibility conditions for a given high-order operator is a fundamental step toward generalizing conservation laws within the context of differential equation theory.

The development of an effective machine learning framework is critical to predicting the complex structure-property relationships inherent to this material. The study's primary objective was to create such a predictive framework by integrating key factors, including 3D-printed part geometry, orientation, infill settings, and photopolymer resin composition. a model is often framed as an online optimization problem. When a model is updated by a single data point at a time, it leads to frequent unnecessary disk access. When a batch of data is utilized for each model update, it results in non-convex loss functions, which hinders the application of efficient optimization techniques. This research introduces a novel method, Passive-Active Learning (PAL), which overcomes these challenges. PAL learns from multiple independent data streams in an online, incremental manner without sacrificing the efficiency of optimization. It achieves this by adaptively selecting data points to minimize a smooth upper bound on the regret, which has a computationally efficient solution that can be computed in parallel. In experiments conducted on the MNIST and ImageNet datasets, PAL has shown promising results, often outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy while requiring less training time.

unique threshold mechanism in an otherwise standard Hotelling-downstream market framework. In this framework, two monopolistic firms, located upstream, compete by setting prices to sell a common good to consumers. Consumers' locations and willingness to pay are randomly determined, adhering to a uniform distribution. The proposed threshold mechanism dictates that consumers only purchase the higher-quality product if it is below a certain price point; otherwise, they either buy the inferior product or remain in the market. We analyze the equilibrium pricing strategies for the upstream firms and find that their optimal approach involves setting prices that allow both the lower-quality and higher-quality products to coexist in the market. A key characteristic of the threshold mechanism is its sensitivity to price, which expires once the higher-quality product becomes too expensive. This feature creates an incentive for firms to invest in quality enhancement. However, the standard economic model of downstream Hotelling fails to capture this investment motivation due to its assumption of a binary consumer choice. In contrast, the proposed threshold mechanism results in a market quality underinvestment issue. Furthermore, the model can be applied to real-world scenarios, such as smartphone markets, and policy implications arise in terms of potential government intervention.

approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission.

High Energy Electromagnetic Counterparty Observer, or DECIDE pipeline is to maximize the likelihood of successfully identifying an electromagnetic counterpart to a gravitational wave signal while minimizing the necessary integration time. This can be accomplished by optimally combining the data from multiple telescopes, each observing the same region of the sky at various wavelengths and time intervals. Although the Decisive Engine for Identifying DECisions, or DECIDE pipeline was initially created to address the challenge of rapidly making informed decisions in the context of the LIGO-VIRGO observations, its decision-making capabilities are not confined to this area. In fact, DECIDE's framework can be applied to a wide range of fields that require making informed decisions under time constraints.

Despite significant computational advancements since then, many learning theory problems remain equally complex, necessitating a reevaluation of the fundamental assumptions made a century ago. To address this, we investigated whether existing statistical learning theories can accommodate the consideration of time within models and their applications. By integrating a general compositional framework for statistical learning with a compelling concept of fluid data, we can model the inherent flow of information. Notably, traditional learning tools such as empirical risk minimization and variational inference have been expanded to accommodate these dynamic environments. To address the issue of targeted collisions involving the initial state in modern SHA-2 functions, our research reveals that reducing the number of hash rounds by a minimal amount can facilitate successful attacks. Specifically, we demonstrate that the TARGET COLLISION RESISTANCE (TCR) of the SHA-256 variant is compromised when reduced to 64 rounds, by presenting a 256-BIT LONG targeted collision attack. Similarly, we showcase a 128-BIT LONG attack on the SHA-224 variant with 56 rounds, resulting in a time complexity of approximately $2^{114.6}$ and a output length of 224 bits. By reducing the number of rounds to 55 in SHA-224, a 128-BIT LONG attack can be executed with a time complexity of approximately $2^{109.5}$. Moreover, our findings can be applied to other SHA-224/256 variants or derivatives that adhere to specific constraints, including the number of bits and round reduction criteria. By utilizing the techniques developed in this study, researchers can expedite the creation of new targeted collision attacks on SHA-2 functions by leveraging the pre-calculated tables we have provided.

Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a reliable method to predict the risky behavior of a human driver, utilizing traffic light timing and a minimum following distance criterion. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.

Memory (LSTM) have found extensive use in time series forecasting due to their sequence processing capabilities. However, standard LSTMs struggle to capture long-range dependencies in highly repetitive time series data. To overcome this limitation, an LSTM variant called ConvLSTM has been developed, which has demonstrated success in modeling long-range dependencies and has been applied to various tasks including weather forecasting and video understanding. Despite these advancements, existing ConvLSTM formulations still face limitations in effectively extracting spatial features. To address this, a new ConvLSTM cell known as DAS-LSTM has been proposed, which fuses the strengths of attention mechanisms and dense connections. Through comprehensive comparative testing on three time series datasets, DAS-LSTM has been shown to outperform ConvLSTM and several other state-of-the-art models in forecasting long-range dependencies, demonstrating significant improvements in performance with minimal increase in computational cost.

However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability and slow model update processes due to large data sizes. In contrast, language models based on small datasets enable flexible inclusion of new vocabulary and knowledge, adaptation to changing linguistic norms, and personalization to individual preferences, despite facing challenges in handling context, coreference, and core semantic understanding. In light of these considerations, we propose a novel architecture, termed ReCoNeSe, that combines data-efficient transfer learning with a neural network, allowing models to manage complex contextual issues. Experiments conducted on the CLSa score-based language disambiguation task demonstrate the superiority of ReCoNeSe in disambiguating entities, coreferencing entities, and producing coherent text, outperforming models trained on larger datasets such as Wikipedia and Google.

At the solstices, a specific north-south pattern of auroral ovals emerges, with the low-latitude oval, influenced by Earth-like magnetospheric activities, usually resides further from the poles than the middle-latitude oval. Studies have shown that this low-latitude oval latitudes decrease during solar periods, largely due to changes in the Sun's activity that affect solar flux. To understand how this pattern applies to Saturn, we need a reliable method to track changes in the low-latitude oval latitude over time. Although historical observations of the aurora on the planet have been limited, particularly between 1888 and 1918, a combination of data from the Hiastron and Cassini missions, along with historical records, have allowed for a correlation analysis of the low-latitude oval latitude and solar periods. Our study shows that, unlike the middle-latitude oval which expands at perihelion, the low-latitude oval narrows, and importantly, reaches its maximum distance from the poles exactly when solar periods reach their peak. This discovery clarifies the complex relationship between the low-latitude oval and oxygen ions, and highlights the importance of more comprehensive historical records of the aurora on Saturn to gain further understanding.

In recent years, there has been an increasing interest in manipulating the 2D materials' surfaces to control electronic devices' performance. As an example, generating electric fields through gate-voltages in field-effect transistors has a limited impact on carrier distribution near the semiconductor's surface due to carrier screening. In this study, we demonstrate that applying pressure to an epitaxial GaAs/GaAlAs two-electron oscillator allows for precise control over carrier localization at the 2D material's surface. By adjusting the pressure, we can transition from confining carriers in an accumulation layer to forming a depletion hole liquid and back to a depletion layer without the use of gate-voltages. Furthermore, we show that applying pressure to an electrostatically disordered GaAs oscillator can restore its mobility and induce the formation of a depletion hole liquid. Finally, we demonstrate the reversibility of both the depletion-to-activation transition and the activation mobility restoration induced by pressure.

Although scattering events are often considered negligible in these methods, research into nonlinear optical responses requires a more detailed understanding of how incident light interacts with matter. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major achievement of our approach, the method achieves second-order order convergence rates in the $H^1$ and $L^2$ norms respectively. Notably, this result is comparable to rates obtained for solutions to ordinary differential equations along the fracture lines or surfaces. Our research also encompasses results for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional scenarios.

To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. This study investigates how this issue impacts the development of neutrino generation models, using neutrinoless double beta decay as a key reference point. This research also outlines the conditions under which double beta decay constraints are applicable and how this knowledge can be utilized to explain observed fluctuations in decay rates. This explanation is then used to motivate the choice of parameter ranges selected for parameter space scanning.

To better understand this phenomenon, new calculation methods are needed that can accurately model the ensemble of gravitational waves generated during cosmological events. In this paper, we introduce a new framework, a perturbed Fourier-space perturbation theory, which is capable of efficiently and accurately describing the evolution of these gravitational wave ensembles. GPU and TPU advancements, have significantly scaled tensor network algorithms for complex quantum simulation and machine learning applications. The quantum-inspired nature of these algorithms makes them mappable to parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), which is now fueling proposals for leveraging near-term quantum devices to solve tractable problems and potentially gain an advantage over classical methods. Furthermore, understanding the underlying mechanisms of training TN models and comparing them to training PQC architectures is essential for utilizing both systems effectively. In this study, we uncover a critical issue hindering the training of matrix product state variational circuits, namely the formation of trainability barriers during the optimization process. By conducting numerical experiments, we confirm that this phenomenon arises due to the development of a highly overconstrained cost function landscape as entanglement increases, causing gradient vanishing and trapping the optimization process in local minima. We also demonstrate the feasibility of mitigating this barrier through the introduction of unitary gates with higher bond dimensions. In addition, we identify another unitary decomposition that is both training-efficient and physically meaningful. These discoveries provide actionable guidelines for developing robust quantum-inspired algorithms and actable principles for designing near-term quantum advantage algorithms.

The proposed concept learning network structure facilitates the discovery of visual concepts from training data and assigns binary concepts to training objects, which are then used as explicit visual inputs to train the intermediate layers of the network. to as the '1.5-order trick', has been extensively analyzed in a simplified context of two real scalars and a real graviton, without the inclusion of fermions.  A novel approach to understanding this trick is examined, emphasizing its inherent limitations.  It becomes apparent that the 1.5-order trick is not a universally applicable method for constructing consistent supergravity theories.  Moreover, a more direct and unambiguous procedure is presented, deviating from the traditional trick.  This alternative method involves incorporating auxiliary fields into the action, where their specific role can be understood through conventional second-order equations of motion.  Although this approach may seem counterintuitive given the inherent non-linearity of these equations, it proves effective in defining the action's variables clearly.  Furthermore, a simpler rationale for employing the 1.5-order trick emerges when viewing the auxiliary fields as participating in a standard second-order dynamics.  Consequently, integrating the auxiliary fields in this manner reduces to performing a partial integration, allowing the derivation of their 'Hamiltonian' conjugate momenta.  The proposed alternative method, however, faces an obstacle in achieving this reduction due to the inevitable appearance of square roots in the resulting action.  This difficulty with square roots contributes to the perceived enigmatic nature of the 1.5-order trick.

Employing projected sensitivities from the muon EDM experiment at the Fermilab/BNL muon storage ring, our findings relate new physics scales to observable outcomes. Existing theoretical estimates for final state muon rates are uncertain at a level exceeding 10%, which corresponds to estimated uncertainties in injected beam intensity. Consequently, detecting a new physics signal will require precise control over final state muon rates, decay time distributions, and angular distributions, as well as injected beam intensity.

We employed the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to observe a specific region of the CMZ, the 30 Doradus Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud, to improve signal-to-noise ratio and avoid radio interference. Our observations over four nights in March-April 2019, as the Earth orbited the Sun, allowed for the measurement of radial velocities in the plane of the galaxy. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

The (strict) positive definiteness of these functions can model phenomena like random walks, zonal functions, and more, on the underlying space. While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share key properties with their spatial counterparts, this study also establishes that the resulting Mat\'ern Gaussian processes on graphs, when $\nu\gt 0.5$, exhibit smooth sample paths and derives the sample path continuity in terms of the $\Leftharpoonup_{\infty}$ norm. This study simultaneously adapts the commonly used metrics, such as the intrinsic spectrum norm and the Euclidean norm, and obtains the corresponding continuity proofs. This research simultaneously contributes to both expanding our theoretical understanding of Gaussian processes and enhancing our capacity to design effective methods for predicting phenomena within the context of graph data.

AR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at higher magnetic fields.

A promising avenue of non-invasive diagnosis involves using AI to analyze contrast-enhanced CT images of tumors. Nevertheless, developing CT-based AI models that can match the accuracy of pathologists is hampered by the lack of precisely labeled data. Existing methods use automated segmentation models to generate CT labels, but they often fail at identifying subtle abnormalities and misclassifying pathological types. In response, we present a novel framework called CT-En-Path-Fine, an efficient multi-stage approach that leverages CT images of surgically removed tumors to accurately classify tumor pathology. This framework starts with an improved segmentation model called EnPathSeg-Net, which utilizes pathological knowledge to extract relevant CT features. It then employs a fine-grained representation learning module to capture CT features relevant to tumor pathology classification. Finally, the framework leverages the extracted features with a multi-task knowledge distillation module that utilizes the pathological model to orient the CT model. Our framework achieves remarkable results, outperforming state-of-the-art methods with a classification accuracy of 90.07% on a lung cancer dataset containing 2880 samples.

We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A graphical representation of GCNNs is also introduced to visually depict their structure and learning process. Moreover, this study shows that GCNNs are capable of replicating the functionality of traditional CNNs and FC NNs. Lastly, a new type of filter called a Matched Filtered Graph Convolutional Network (MFCNN) is proposed as an intuitive GCNN architecture and has been tested on various datasets, outperforming other models.

gravity can be reformulated as a theory of group elements based on an affine bundle, which becomes equivalent to Einstein-Cartan theory. This redundancy can be leveraged to apply a method from higher-spin gravity, specifically using the Vassilevich-Viroda action in its first-order form. By utilizing this method, we can determine the two-point function for a specific type of gravitational field, known as a symmetric rank-2 tensor, while excluding spin-5/2 fermionic fields. This calculation aligns with previous findings, even though those results were obtained in different contexts using distinct methods. Additionally, this approach can be adapted to theories of Einstein-Hilbert type with an arbitrary coefficient for the $C^3$ cubic term, which corresponds to a parameter in the higher-spin theory. By making this adjustment, we can make small changes to the Einstein Hilbert action, such as adding an infinite number of multi-trace interactions, without making the theory inconsistent. As a result, linearized gravity remains a viable approach in three-dimensional spacetime, in contrast to situations in four-dimensional spacetime, where such theories typically break down due to the nonexistence of free higher-spin bosonic fields.

a circularly polarized light beam incident on the edge of a disk made of a type-A metamaterial can experience a surprising transverse acceleration, causing it to rotate in the same direction as its orbital angular momentum, regardless of the polarization handedness. This countervailing behavior, resulting from the superposition of two counteracting effects, can be precisely controlled by adjusting the size of the disk or the frequency of the light, and arises regardless of the light's intensity or the material's absorption properties. By leveraging this phenomenon, we propose a practical, compact device that can switch the rotational direction of light based on its circular polarization, and by extending the design to a metamaterial strip, we enable the switching of the orbital angular momentum as well. These findings provide the fundamental groundwork for developing all-optical multiplexing and switching devices in the fields of high-speed optical communication and all-optical computing.

To showcase the difficulty of this classification task, we also present a baseline deep learning network and discuss the challenges associated with this classification problem.

Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. It demonstrates that the relative I-functions remain consistent across these transformations, with certain parameters remaining unchanged. It also establishes that the relative Gromov-Witten theory for a particular class of toric varieties is equivalent among them. It derives this equivalence from analyzing the behavior of relative I-functions at specific singular points and utilizing symmetries in Fock spaces to map the contours during toric transformations. This approach is extended to handle certain equivariant toric flips and shows that the relative I-functions are analytic continuations of one another across these transformations. This result can be utilized to simplify calculations of relative I-functions for toric complete intersections and shows that their S-duality properties are equivalent to those of toric complete intersections.

To develop a GAN variant for this purpose, the basic model is expanded to incorporate the classification of oriented text. To train this extended model, an approach is proposed to create an oriented version of the LeSOT training set, which involves attaching orientation labels to existing data and further dividing images based on text orientation.
